task.goal: Create a reusable community-theater scene transition with only light and movement.
hard_constraints: Five performers, a black-box room and one technician; no new set purchase.
Transition must keep aisles clear and take under 40 seconds.
Evaluate audience comprehension, performer load and repeatability at two rehearsals.
task.available_resources: Existing portable lamps and rehearsal notes.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Light handoff between two places
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a change in the location of light to tell the audience that the scene has moved. Before the performance, place two existing portable lamps outside performer routes, aimed at separate areas within the playing space. Keep cables against the room boundary and all aisles clear. The five performers finish the outgoing scene clustered in area A. The technician switches on lamp B; performers turn toward it, then cross directly into their opening positions for the next scene. Once everyone has left A, the technician switches off lamp A. Hold the new arrangement for three seconds before dialogue begins. Budget 25–30 seconds, including the crossing.

The working principle is a visible transfer of attention: the destination becomes legible before the actors arrive. Reuse the same sequence for later transitions, reversing direction as needed. Required resources are two existing independently switchable lamps, safe fixed positions, and a cue sequence recorded in rehearsal notes. No dimmer or blackout is necessary. This assumes the lamps create distinguishable areas under the room’s ambient light and one technician can operate both from a safe position. It communicates a change of place more reliably than the identity of that place; the next scene’s opening arrangement must supply that detail.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, show this transition and a comparator using the same crossing under steady light to a few observers unfamiliar with the staging. Ask where their attention went and whether the scene changed location. Time both versions and ask each performer to rate effort and cue uncertainty. At rehearsal two, repeat the chosen sequence three times after running the preceding scene. Record duration, missed cues, route conflicts and comprehension in rehearsal notes. Reject or simplify it if the lighting adds no clarity, any run reaches 40 seconds, or operation requires the technician to enter an aisle.

DIRECT_FULL.title: The ensemble redraws the room
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Keep the light steady and transform the performers’ spatial relationships into the architecture of the next scene. For example, five performers end as a tight inward-facing group; over three counted phrases they open into two opposing pairs and a fifth person between them, establishing a hearing, confrontation or formal meeting. Each performer takes a short direct route entirely inside the playing area. They stop together, orient their gaze toward the new focal person and hold for three seconds. Budget 20–25 seconds.

The mechanism is a change in social geometry: proximity, facing and status make the new situation visible without moving scenery. For reuse, give each recurring location one distinctive opening formation and write the five routes in rehearsal notes. Adapt formations to the actual script rather than adding unexplained symbolic gestures. An existing lamp can provide steady illumination; the technician maintains the state and watches for unsafe visibility.

This needs enough internal floor space for five short routes and performers who can sustain clear, comfortable positions. It requires no lamp switching, furniture, props or purchases. Its limit is specificity: bodies can establish a relationship or type of space, but may not distinguish two otherwise similar rooms. Avoid making performers hold strenuous poses as imaginary scenery. The outcome depends on a readable difference between the outgoing and incoming formations.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, compare the designed transformation with an ordinary walk to the same opening positions, using identical lighting and no dialogue. Ask unfamiliar observers to describe the resulting relationships and whether they recognized a new scene. Collect performer effort ratings and identify difficult crossings. At rehearsal two, run the transformation three times from the preceding scene, checking duration, position accuracy and synchronized arrival. Keep it only if observers understand the intended relationship at least as well as with the comparator and the formation remains comfortable and repeatable below 40 seconds.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A movement phrase marks a jump in time
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a repeated action with a changed ending to signal that time has passed. Choose one short, script-relevant movement available to all five performers, such as turning toward an imagined doorway. At the outgoing scene’s end, everyone performs it once at ordinary speed, resets in place, then repeats it slowly. During the slow repetition they change posture and facing into the next scene’s opening state. Hold that final image for three seconds before speech. Keep the complete sequence to 18–25 seconds, with no travel outside the playing area.

The mechanism is repetition followed by visible difference: the audience sees an earlier moment recur and resolve into a later condition. Establish the convention at its first use, then retain the same phrase and rhythm for later time jumps. An existing portable lamp provides steady light, leaving the technician one stable state to maintain. Record the phrase, counts and final positions in rehearsal notes.

This assumes the script contains a meaningful before-and-after contrast that the performers can show physically. Small changes in energy, gaze or stance should express character circumstances rather than rely on age stereotypes. It works best for elapsed time, memory or recurring routines; it may confuse audiences if used indiscriminately for changes of location. Its principal uncertainty is whether repetition reads as a transition or as action continuing within the same scene. No new equipment, sound or set is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: At rehearsal one, show unfamiliar observers the repeated phrase and a comparator consisting of a simple pause followed by the same new posture. Ask whether time passed, whether the scene changed and what physical difference they noticed. Ask performers about counting difficulty and physical effort. At rehearsal two, repeat the transition three times after the outgoing scene and record duration, synchronization errors and effort. Reject the device if observers consistently interpret it as continuous action, or if the repetition adds performer load without improving comprehension. Every run must stay below 40 seconds with aisles clear.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A dark interval closes the scene
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use a brief interruption of visibility as a reusable boundary between scenes. The five performers freeze at the outgoing scene’s final moment. The technician switches off the existing performance lamps for two seconds while everyone remains still, then restores the same lighting. Under restored light, performers release character posture and walk directly to their next opening positions within the playing area. They settle, take one shared breath and begin the next scene. Budget 15–25 seconds, including the dark interval and reset.

The mechanism is visual punctuation: briefly removing the stage image closes the preceding scene, allowing the subsequent movement to read as a reset. Unlike a transfer between illuminated locations, this convention can mark a scene boundary even when both scenes occupy the same space. It does not by itself explain a new location or how much time has passed; the next scene must establish those details.

Use only existing lamps, fixed safely outside walking routes, with cables secured away from aisles. Record the freeze, lighting cues and five short routes in rehearsal notes. One technician must be able to switch the relevant lamps safely from a single position. Keep required exit and aisle illumination operating throughout. No performer moves during the dark interval, and travel begins only when visibility returns.

This assumes the existing lamps permit a clearly perceptible interruption without interfering with safety lighting. If ambient light makes the interruption barely noticeable, or the lamps cannot be controlled together, this mechanism may not be practical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
At rehearsal one, show a few unfamiliar observers the outgoing scene ending and incoming opening, first with a lit pause and then with the dark interval; reverse the order for some observers if feasible. Keep routes and timing otherwise identical. Ask whether they perceived a scene boundary and whether the reset looked intentional. Collect performer effort and cue-confidence ratings, and note technician workload.

At rehearsal two, repeat both versions after the preceding scene. Time three runs of the proposed transition and record missed freezes, premature movement, route conflicts and observer interpretations. Reject the dark interval if it adds confusion or offers no clearer boundary than the lit pause. Require every run to finish below 40 seconds, aisles to remain clear, and performers to report manageable effort and reliable cues at both rehearsals.

DIRECT_FULL.title: A shadow landmark establishes the next place
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
Use enlarged shadows as temporary scenery. For a transition into a passage or enclosed meeting place, two performers stand apart near a fixed portable lamp so their shadows form tall sides of an opening on an existing plain wall. They keep their arms comfortably lowered; the gap between their shadows supplies the doorway. The other three performers approach that opening within the playing area and settle into the next scene’s opening positions. Hold the image for three seconds, then let the two shadow makers step away from the beam and join the scene. Target 20–30 seconds.

The mechanism is optical enlargement: ordinary bodies briefly become an architectural landmark, giving the incoming action a visible destination without scenery. Unlike a formation that communicates social relationships, the projected image supplies a spatial feature. Reuse the doorway for recurring entrances or enclosed locations, retaining its proportions and approach direction.

This requires an existing lamp that produces reasonably distinct shadows, a suitable wall, and enough space to keep performers safely away from the lamp. Fix the lamp outside all routes, keep cables and performers clear of aisles, and preserve required safety lighting. One technician switches it on at the outgoing scene’s final stillness and off after the arrival image; existing general illumination must remain sufficient for movement. Record lamp position, performer positions and cues in rehearsal notes. No purchases, props, sound or strenuous holds are needed.

The main uncertainty is whether available lamps and ambient light produce a recognizable opening. This mechanism suits scripts with a meaningful threshold; it cannot reliably identify a particular building. Reject it if achieving a readable shadow requires unsafe proximity, obstructing an aisle or an uncomfortable stance.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment:
At rehearsal one, first inspect shadow clarity from the actual audience positions. Then show a few unfamiliar observers the transition and a simple comparator: the same arrivals under steady light without the shadow doorway. Ask what spatial feature they perceived and whether the arrival established a new place. Record duration, each performer’s effort and cue uncertainty, and technician difficulty.

At rehearsal two, repeat both versions after the preceding scene, including three timed runs of the shadow version. Again collect audience interpretations and performer effort ratings; record missed positions, inconsistent shadows and cue errors. Keep the device only if the doorway improves spatial comprehension, the workload remains manageable, and all three runs reproduce the image with clear aisles in under 40 seconds.

EXPAND.title: A brief dark cut hides the reset
EXPAND.proposal:
Use a short interruption of visibility to separate scenes while concealing a small reset. Unlike the prior light handoff, the destination is never illuminated before the performers arrive: the audience sees one completed image, then a different image after a cut.

Before starting, the technician places existing lamps in fixed positions outside aisles, with cables outside movement routes. All five performers choose their next positions within one comfortable step of their outgoing positions. Rehearse those steps in full light. At the outgoing scene’s final stillness, the technician switches off the acting lamps. Performers make their single steps, change facing and settle. After a fixed four-count, the technician restores the same lighting. Everyone holds the new image for three seconds before dialogue. Allow 12–18 seconds overall.

The mechanism is interruption of visual continuity: the hidden change lets spectators infer a new scene without watching actors relocate. It needs lamps that can be switched together from the technician’s station, a sufficiently noticeable reduction in light, and safe footing. Nobody moves lamps during the transition. Emergency lighting remains untouched.

Use this only where each performer can execute a short, unobstructed step safely under the remaining light. If that is impossible, this route is unsuitable. If the light fails to return, performers stay still; the technician restores a usable state before action resumes. The method may communicate a scene boundary clearly while conveying little about the new location, which must become understandable from the opening action.
EXPAND.experiment: The technician owns a two-rehearsal trial. At rehearsal one, compare the cut with the prior illuminated handoff using the same outgoing and incoming scenes. Ask unfamiliar observers whether a new scene began and where they believe it occurs; collect performer effort and confidence ratings. Stop immediately for uncertain footing or an obstructed route. At rehearsal two, run each version three times after the preceding scene, recording duration, early movement, light-operation errors and comprehension. Drop the cut if any run reaches 40 seconds, or if its clarity is no better while darkness increases performer uncertainty. Record the selected counts and recovery instruction in rehearsal notes.

EXPAND.title: Carry one unfinished action across the scene boundary
EXPAND.proposal:
Connect two scenes through one continuous action whose meaning changes when it finishes. For example, if the script supports it, a performer begins reaching toward someone in the outgoing scene and completes that reach toward a different person in the incoming scene. The audience follows the action across the change.

Choose an actual compatible action from the script; do not add a mysterious gesture solely to enable the transition. Keep existing lamps steady, safely positioned with clear aisles and cables outside routes. At the outgoing scene’s end, the focal performer begins the reach. During its uninterrupted six-count extension, the other four performers take short rehearsed routes within the playing area and assume their next roles or relationships. The focal performer completes the reach in the new situation. Its recipient responds, starting the next scene. Target 12–20 seconds, including a brief settling moment.

The mechanism is continuity of attention: an unresolved action gives spectators something meaningful to follow while the surrounding context changes. Unlike the prior repeated time-jump phrase, the action happens once and does not reset. Unlike the light handoff, attention stays with a performer.

This requires a script-compatible connection and unobstructed internal routes. It suits linked scenes better than unrelated locations and may imply a thematic connection the production does not intend. The technician maintains usable steady illumination. If someone arrives late, the focal performer pauses comfortably before completing the action; after one extra four-count, complete it and start the scene without attempting the transition again. Record the action, routes and receiving cue in rehearsal notes.
EXPAND.experiment: A designated performer leads the trial at both rehearsals. At rehearsal one, compare the continuous action with the prior ordinary formation change under identical steady light. Ask unfamiliar observers what happened, whether the scene changed and whether they inferred an unintended connection. Collect effort and cue-confidence ratings from all five performers. Reject the device if no natural action fits. At rehearsal two, repeat both versions three times from the preceding scene, including one deliberately late arrival to inspect recovery. Stop for route interference or a duration of 40 seconds. Keep the bridge only if it improves attention or comprehension without increasing missed entrances, uncomfortable holds or misleading interpretations.

EXPAND.title: Let a shared physical condition reveal the new place
EXPAND.proposal:
Make the next environment visible through the same external force acting on all five performers. For a script-supported exterior, for example, everyone encounters a strong headwind as the outgoing scene ends. Their common direction of resistance establishes an outdoor condition before dialogue supplies the exact location.

Choose one condition already justified by the next scene, such as wind or a cramped low passage. Assign a simple, comfortable physical response to each performer. With existing lamps held steady, the performers release the outgoing scene together. Over four counts, they encounter the condition; over eight more, they travel along short, separate routes inside the playing area while responding consistently to it. They reach their opening positions, reduce the response to a sustainable level and begin the next scene. Target 18–25 seconds. Lamps remain fixed, with cables outside routes and all aisles clear.

The mechanism is a shared physical cause: matching reactions let spectators infer an unseen environment. It supplies information that a light handoff alone cannot supply. Unlike the prior social-geometry route, the environmental meaning should remain readable even if the performers’ arrangement changes.

This requires a next scene with a distinctive, playable condition. It cannot reliably distinguish arbitrary indoor rooms, and exaggerated movement could turn a serious transition comic. Avoid actual loss of balance, strenuous crouches or contact between performers. The technician maintains steady visibility. If timing separates, each performer continues the same modest response until the designated lead reaches the opening position and settles; that visible settling starts dialogue. Record the shared direction, intensity, paths and lead cue in rehearsal notes.
EXPAND.experiment: The designated lead owns the trial. At rehearsal one, show unfamiliar observers this version and the prior light handoff into the same scene. Ask what environment they inferred, whether the scene changed and what tone they perceived. Have performers rate effort and concentration; stop for discomfort or unstable movement. At rehearsal two, repeat both versions three times after the preceding scene. Record duration, inconsistent force direction, missed settling cues and observer comprehension. Reject the environmental version if it adds no useful setting information, introduces unwanted comedy or raises performer load substantially. Every run must stay below 40 seconds with clear aisles; simplify the movement before retaining it.

EXPAND.title: Light handoff with a visible acceptance cue
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “Light handoff between two places.” Preserve its two fixed light areas, short internal crossing and three-second arrival hold. Add a destination acceptance rule: performers remain in the outgoing scene until lamp B is visibly on and the designated lead turns toward it. The technician owns lighting readiness; the lead owns starting movement only after acceptance. This prevents a missed lamp cue from sending five people toward an unreadable destination.

Use two existing independently switchable lamps, with cables outside routes and aisles. The technician lights B while leaving A on; the lead checks the visible destination, turns, and all five cross along rehearsed paths. The technician extinguishes A only after the last performer clears it. Target 25–30 seconds.

If B fails to light within a rehearsed four-count, the lead starts an ordinary crossing under A, provided A illuminates the whole route; the technician leaves A on. If that fallback route lacks usable illumination during setup, this mechanism is unsuitable. If movement is interrupted, leave both working lamps on and let performers walk directly to their destinations without restarting the effect. Rehearsal must establish that this recovery finishes within 35 seconds; otherwise shorten the routes.

This assumes distinguishable light areas and safe operation from one technician’s position. Compared with the source, it adds one lead check and a brief possible wait, but gives responsibility and recovery to an otherwise implicit handoff. It communicates relocation more readily than a specific address; the incoming action must establish that detail.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the technician and designated lead run one normal transition and one simulated destination-lamp failure, with the fallback still safely illuminated. Time each from outgoing stillness to readiness for dialogue. Ask unfamiliar observers whether the scene changed location and where their attention went; ask all five performers for effort and cue-confidence ratings. Stop immediately for uncertain footing, an aisle intrusion or insufficient light. At rehearsal two, run three transitions from the preceding scene, including one interrupted crossing. Record comprehension, duration, missed cues and performer load in existing notes. Retain only if every run finishes below 40 seconds and the failure procedure is executable without extra prompting. Compare normal operation with the original handoff: the added acceptance cue should earn its small delay through clearer starts or fewer cue errors; that benefit remains untested.

EXPAND.title: Redraw the room with routes that cannot intersect
EXPAND.proposal:
Upgrade source: “The ensemble redraws the room.” Preserve steady lighting, a distinctive incoming social formation, comfortable poses and a three-second final hold. Change route assignment: before adopting a formation, the designated performer lead must find five short paths that do not intersect or pass through another performer’s waiting position. Change which performer occupies an interchangeable destination where the script permits. This addresses collisions during imperfect timing, which synchronized arrival alone does not prevent.

For example, transform an inward-facing cluster into two opposing pairs with a fifth person between them. Everyone opens along separate paths inside the playing area, then directs attention toward the focal person. Target 20–25 seconds. The technician maintains usable steady illumination from an existing fixed lamp; record paths and destinations in rehearsal notes. No purchases or floor markings are required.

The adoption boundary is practical: each performer must be able to stop anywhere on their route without blocking someone else. If the formation fails that check, reduce travel or choose another script-compatible formation before using it. If no distinct formation meets it, use a plain, rehearsed walk to the next scene and accept the loss of the visual device. During an interruption, performers keep comfortable positions; the lead resumes the unfinished opening once space is clear, without returning to the cluster. Shorten the movement if this recovery cannot finish within 35 seconds.

The mechanism remains social geometry: relationships establish the incoming situation. Compared with the source, route design takes more preparation and restricts available formations, but should reduce reliance on precise synchronization. It still cannot reliably identify two socially similar rooms.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the performer lead checks each route with one person deliberately pausing midway while the others continue. Stop for any blocked path, contact, discomfort or aisle intrusion; revise the formation before repeating. Show the resulting transition and a plain walk to the same positions to unfamiliar observers. Ask whether a new scene began and what relationships they inferred; collect effort and concentration ratings from all five performers. At rehearsal two, run three times after the preceding scene, including one delayed start. Record duration, route conflicts, arrival accuracy, comprehension and performer load. Keep the device only if every run stays below 40 seconds, recovery needs no spoken instruction, and observers understand the intended relationships at least as well as with the plain walk.

EXPAND.title: A repeated light signature becomes the scene-boundary signal
EXPAND.proposal:
Use an invariant light rhythm as theatrical punctuation. Its working principle is a learned convention: the same visible signal comes to mean “a new scene begins,” regardless of location, formation or elapsed story time.

Keep one existing lamp on continuously so all five performers and their routes remain visible. Position a second, independently switched lamp where its contribution is noticeable but does not shine into spectators’ eyes. At the outgoing scene’s final stillness, the technician switches the accent lamp on for two counts, off for two, on for two, then off. During this signature, performers release character tension and walk normally to the incoming positions inside the playing area. They settle for three seconds, then begin. Target 15–25 seconds. Repeat the identical signature at subsequent scene boundaries so the association can develop. The first incoming scene must make its changed situation understandable through its opening action.

This requires two suitable existing lamps, safe fixed cabling, convenient switching and enough baseline light for the whole reset. Avoid rapid flashing; use only lamps suitable for repeated ordinary switching. The technician owns the signature, while a designated performer owns the final settling cue. If an accent cue is missed, do not restart the rhythm: finish the ordinary walk under the base lamp and begin from the settled image. If the accent is imperceptible or its switching is awkward, drop it and use that same plain reset.

Unlike changing the destination of light or hiding movement in darkness, this mechanism marks a boundary through an acquired signal while the reset stays visible. Compared with a plain walk, it adds technician work and may initially resemble an accidental lighting change. Its potential benefit is one reusable boundary cue across otherwise unrelated scenes; it supplies no location information by itself.
EXPAND.experiment: At rehearsal one, the technician presents three short scene endings and beginnings using the signature, with all five performers. Ask unfamiliar observers after each when they thought a new scene began and what they believed changed. Compare with the same resets under steady light; collect performer effort and cue-confidence ratings and technician switching difficulty. Stop for visual discomfort, inadequate baseline visibility or aisle intrusion. At rehearsal two, repeat the three boundaries from their preceding scenes, including one intentionally omitted accent cue. Record comprehension, duration, performer load and cue errors in rehearsal notes. Retain only if every transition stays below 40 seconds, the omitted cue does not stall action, and observers increasingly recognize the boundary without being told the code. If no useful recognition develops, remove the accent sequence; its added operation is then unjustified.
